subject: Vocabulary
topic: Foreign Words Used in English (W11 B2)

questions.stem: What does the French/Latin term 'STATUS QUO' mean?

options.option_text: The existing or current state of affairs
A formal agreement between two parties

questions.explanation: B is correct. STATUS QUO (Latin) = 'the state in which' — the current or existing state of affairs; the situation as it is now. Example: 'The politicians preferred to maintain the status quo rather than introduce reforms.' Trap: 'New and improved' = opposite of status quo (which implies no change); 'official position' = unrelated; 'formal agreement' = 'quid pro quo' or 'memorandum of understanding', not status quo.

B is correct. BONA FIDE (Latin) = 'in good faith' — genuine, real, authentic, without any deception or fraud. Example: 'She is a bona fide expert in the field.' Trap: 'Done in bad faith' = the OPPOSITE of bona fide; 'official document' = 'bona fide certificate' exists but bona fide itself doesn't mean 'document'.

questions.stem: What does 'DE FACTO' mean, as used in the sentence: 'She is the de facto leader of the organisation'?

options.option_text: The leader in practice, even if not officially recognised

questions.explanation: B is correct. DE FACTO (Latin) = 'in fact' — existing or happening in practice even if not legally or officially established. Contrast with DE JURE (= 'by law'). Example: 'She is the de facto leader' = she actually runs things regardless of who holds the official title. Trap: 'Legally appointed' = DE JURE (the opposite); 'Temporary' and 'Popular' = unrelated to de facto.

questions.stem: What does the term 'AD HOC' mean?
questions.explanation: B is correct. AD HOC (Latin) = 'for this' — created or done for a particular purpose as necessary, not planned in advance; improvised. Example: 'An ad hoc committee was formed to address the crisis' = formed specifically for this one task, not a permanent body. Trap: 'Planned and systematic' = opposite of ad hoc; 'official and permanent' = also opposite; 'repeated' = the opposite of the one-off nature of ad hoc.

options.option_text: A blank document with no value
Complete authority to act as one sees fit

questions.explanation: C is correct. CARTE BLANCHE (French) = literally 'blank card/paper' — unconditional authority to do whatever one wishes; complete freedom of action. Example: 'The president gave the committee carte blanche to restructure the department.' Trap: 'Blank document' = the literal translation (not the figurative idiom meaning); 'White credit card' = superficially literal (wrong).

questions.stem: What does 'PRIMA FACIE' mean in the legal context?

options.option_text: Based on first impression; accepted as correct unless proved otherwise
Based on multiple pieces of evidence

questions.explanation: B is correct. PRIMA FACIE (Latin) = 'at first sight/first face' — based on the first impression; accepted as correct until disproved. In law, a prima facie case = enough evidence on first examination to suggest the defendant may be guilty (not a final verdict). Example: 'There is prima facie evidence of fraud.' Trap: 'Beyond reasonable doubt' = the standard for CONVICTION (very high threshold); prima facie is a much lower threshold (mere initial appearances).

options.option_text: Something given or received for something else in return; an exchange

questions.explanation: A is correct. QUID PRO QUO (Latin) = 'something for something' — a favour or advantage granted in return for something; an exchange of equal value. Example: 'The agreement was a quid pro quo — India opened its market in exchange for trade concessions.' Trap: 'Unconditional gift' = the opposite (quid pro quo always implies a condition/exchange); compare with 'pro bono' (for the public good, without payment).

options.option_text: An accomplished fact; a done deal that cannot be reversed
An agreement that is yet to be ratified

questions.explanation: B is correct. FAIT ACCOMPLI (French) = 'accomplished fact' — something that has already happened and cannot be undone; a done deal. Example: 'By the time the Parliament debated it, the merger was a fait accompli.' The key element: it's too late to alter or oppose it. Trap: 'Perfectly completed task' = misses the 'irreversibility' aspect; 'planned future action' = opposite (fait accompli is ALREADY done); 'yet to be ratified' = opposite.

options.option_text: As it is; in the same condition
With the main terms reversed; the other way around
By the very fact; by the act itself

questions.explanation: B is correct. VICE VERSA (Latin) = 'with position turned about' — used to indicate that the order of a statement can be reversed and the meaning remains valid. Example: 'Teachers influence students and vice versa' = students also influence teachers (reversed). Trap: 'As it is' = 'status quo' or 'in situ'; 'instead of' = 'in lieu of' or 'vice' in some contexts; 'by the act itself' = 'ipso facto'.

questions.stem: What does 'PRO BONO' mean when a lawyer works 'pro bono'?

options.option_text: For the public good; without charge

questions.explanation: B is correct. PRO BONO (Latin, short for 'pro bono publico') = 'for the public good' — professional work done voluntarily and without payment. Lawyers who work pro bono provide free legal services to clients who cannot afford them. Example: 'The law firm dedicated 5% of their work to pro bono cases.' Trap: 'On behalf of government' = 'pro rege' or similar; 'Bonus scheme' = confused with the English word 'bonus' (which has a different Latin root).
